name: Minnesota
overview: Minnesota does not sell tax liens to investors. When delinquent property taxes go unpaid through the redemption period, the land forfeits to the State of Minnesota, which holds it in trust for the local taxing districts. The county board then classifies each forfeited parcel as conservation or nonconservation, and the county auditor may offer nonconservation land for sale at a public auction at the county seat. A parcel cannot be sold for less than its appraised value, except in a later sale the county authorizes under the statute, and the sale is for cash unless the county board has adopted terms, which require at least 10 percent down. The buyer is entitled to immediate possession. Counties may also sell unsold parcels over the counter after an auction. Former owners and lienholders may be able to claim surplus proceeds from a sale.

overview_sources.quote: Parcels of land becoming the property of the state in trust under law declaring the forfeiture of lands to the state for taxes must be classified by the county board of the county in which the parcels lie as conservation or nonconservation.
The sale must not be for less than the appraised value except as provided in subdivision 7a.
a payment of at least ten percent of the purchase price must be made at the time of purchase
The purchaser is entitled to immediate possession, subject to the provisions of any existing valid lease made in behalf of the state.
Any parcels that do not receive a bid during the public sale may be purchased over the counter for 30 days following the auction.
This money can be claimed by former owners and interested parties.
